contentBlocks.body: A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The guarantees are ACID: Atomicity (all of it happens or none of it does), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work, to a degree set by the isolation level), and Durability (once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash, because it is in the write-ahead log).

Without XACT_ABORT, SQL Server aborts only the failing statement for many errors (such as a constraint violation) and keeps going, so the first UPDATE could commit without the second. Use SET XACT_ABORT ON, or TRY...CATCH with ROLLBACK, in any hand-written T-SQL transaction.
Keep transactions short. Locks are held until COMMIT, so never wait on an HTTP call, a message queue, or user input inside one. Do the slow work first, then open the transaction, write, and commit.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Model `SET XACT_ABORT ON; BEGIN TRAN; <one UPDATE pair per transfer>; COMMIT`. Apply transfers in order to a copy of the balances. If a transfer names an account that does not exist, or would make a balance negative (CHECK balance >= 0), roll back everything and return { committed: false, balances: <the original balances> }. Otherwise return { committed: true, balances: <new balances> }. Keep the balances object's key order.
Which ACID property guarantees that a transfer never debits one account without crediting the other?

payload.explanation: Atomicity means all statements in the transaction take effect or none do. Consistency is about constraints holding; isolation is about concurrent transactions; durability is about surviving crashes after commit.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Finish the transaction so its changes become permanent.

payload.text: BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1'; INSERT INTO sales (sku) VALUES ('A1'); ____ TRANSACTION;

knowledgeItems.prompt: In EF Core, you call SaveChangesAsync once after adding an order and its three items. Do you need an explicit transaction?

choices: Yes. Each INSERT commits separately without one
No. A single SaveChanges already wraps all its INSERTs in one transaction
Yes. EF Core never uses transactions by default
Only when the database is SQLite
payload.answer: No. A single SaveChanges already wraps all its INSERTs in one transaction
payload.explanation: EF Core runs each SaveChanges in a transaction when the provider supports it. You need BeginTransaction when several SaveChanges calls, or raw SQL plus SaveChanges, must succeed or fail together.
